guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
“And So That’s the Way It Happened!”

My ex, Xandria, taught me to append “And so that’s the way it happened!” to a difficult memory. “Once upon a time…” can also help if you have trouble starting. It makes the event feel more like a passage in a life story than a trial still in progress.

Try it with a manageable memory. It doesn’t make the memory fiction, prove its accuracy, excuse harm, or cancel repair. If the narrator becomes sneering, shame increases, or you feel unreal, stop rather than adding more distance. If the phrase helps, let it stay short. You can also ask what the person in that story needs from you now.
note: Turn 65 (2026-10-17): Simple Practices, practice 5 of 9 (And So That’s the Way It Happened!), for the dedup.
length: one paragraph or two, about the guide's length less what's already said
before: If talking to your little one or picturing them just gets you silence, try paper. Your wrong hand writes for them (it'll look like a ransom note, so you know it's working), and your good hand writes back as the grown-up who's on their side. Sometimes the protective part grabs the pen first. Let it. It gets the wrong hand until it's had its say.

brief:
- the main point: tell a hard memory like a story and end it with "And so that's the way it happened!" (or start with "Once upon a time…" if starting is hard); it makes the event feel like a passage in a life story rather than a trial still in progress; try it with a manageable memory; it doesn't make the memory fiction or prove it accurate; stop, rather than adding more distance, if the narrator turns sneering, shame increases or you feel unreal; if the phrase helps, keep it short.
- what the dedup leaves to add (experiments/t65-guide/SP-DEDUP-REPORT.md, G5): both phrases and the story-not-trial effect; a manageable memory; neither fiction nor proof; the stop signs (sneering, more shame, feeling unreal), adding no distance; keeping it short.
- already in the article, so not said again: it doesn't excuse harm or cancel repair ("that may need repair"); what the person in the story needs now ("What does Little Joel need right now?").
- E159: "My ex, Xandria, taught me" is the AI guide's first person; the article's ex is unnamed; left out and listed for Joel.
